<form class="book-practice" id="quiz-p07" data-practice-set="P07" novalidate>
<p id="quiz-p07-instructions">Choose one answer for each of the 10 questions. Complete the set, then select <strong>Check answers</strong> to see your score and explanations. Each question is worth one point.</p>
<noscript><p>For a self-check without JavaScript, record your choices, then open the answer key below.</p></noscript>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-01" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">1.</span> People remember to apply for a service and want it, but cannot complete a required identity check on their phones. Which change best matches the observed barrier?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-a" name="p07-01" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Send more reminders about why the service matters.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-b" name="p07-01" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Assume abandonment reveals lack of interest.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-c" name="p07-01" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Provide a workable identity-check route on the devices people use.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-d" name="p07-01" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Hide the identity requirement until the final step.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-01-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-01-e" name="p07-01" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Increase the number of motivational slogans.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-01-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-02" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">2.</span> Two teams share the same rain forecast but choose different umbrella policies because carrying an umbrella has different costs for them. What does this illustrate?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-a" name="p07-02" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Decision costs should be removed from the analysis.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-b" name="p07-02" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Forecast accuracy determines a unique policy for every person.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-c" name="p07-02" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A shared prediction can support different decisions when consequences differ.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-d" name="p07-02" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> One forecast must be numerically incorrect.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-02-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-02-e" name="p07-02" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The teams must disagree about the definition of rain.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-02-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-03" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">3.</span> One intervention sends a reminder at the intended action time. Another is a voluntarily chosen restriction preventing access to a competing activity. Which distinction is correct?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-a" name="p07-03" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Both are informational defaults.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-b" name="p07-03" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Both establish that a habit has already formed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-c" name="p07-03" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> The first removes choice; the second only changes wording.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-d" name="p07-03" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> The first is a mandate; the second is merely a prediction.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-03-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-03-e" name="p07-03" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The first prompts action; the second is a commitment device.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-03-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-04" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">4.</span> A panel records human estimates before seeing an AI forecast. They disagree strongly. Which next step best uses this disagreement?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-a" name="p07-04" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Accept whichever estimate is stated with more confidence.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-b" name="p07-04" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Average the estimates automatically without inspecting shared errors.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-c" name="p07-04" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Choose the AI because computational complexity establishes validity.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-d" name="p07-04" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Replace the recorded human estimates with their post-AI revisions.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-04-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-04-e" name="p07-04" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Check inputs and assumptions, then compare both methods on relevant cases.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-04-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-05" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">5.</span> A redesigned application page increases submissions but also increases ineligible applications and processing delays. Which evaluation best assesses the full decision path?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-a" name="p07-05" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Evaluate only whether the button was clicked faster.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-b" name="p07-05" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Assume higher activity guarantees higher welfare.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-c" name="p07-05" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Track submissions, eligibility, actual service delivery, delays, and user costs.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-d" name="p07-05" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Use submission counts as the sole success measure.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-05-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-05-e" name="p07-05" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Drop ineligible applications from every report without recording them.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-05-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-06" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">6.</span> A team wants to test a new decision aid. Which plan best supports learning whether it improves the current process?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-a" name="p07-06" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Keep only examples where the aid and manager agreed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-b" name="p07-06" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Compare easy cases using the aid with hard cases under the old process.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-c" name="p07-06" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Replace the original records with the aid&#x27;s rewritten summaries.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-d" name="p07-06" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Choose the success metric after seeing which result looks best.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-06-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-06-e" name="p07-06" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Predefine outcomes and randomly assign comparable cases to the two workflows.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-06-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-07" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">7.</span> A reader can exercise safely and remembers the plan, but finds sessions dull. She wants to keep flexible timing and avoid financial penalties. Which design best matches these preferences?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-a" name="p07-07" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Require a forfeitable deposit for missing a scheduled session.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-b" name="p07-07" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Repeat instruction on an exercise she already performs correctly.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-c" name="p07-07" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Publish a league table of other people&#x27;s attendance.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-d" name="p07-07" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Add an extra reminder at a fixed time every day.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-07-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-07-e" name="p07-07" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Pair exercise with a favorite audiobook reserved for those sessions.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-07-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-08" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">8.</span> A model recommends denying a request, but its training labels reflect past administrative decisions that may contain errors. What is the most important governance step?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-a" name="p07-08" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Treat past labels as correct because they are numerous.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-b" name="p07-08" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Audit labels and criteria; assign an accountable owner and review route.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-c" name="p07-08" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Use a more fluent explanation instead of checking the label process.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-d" name="p07-08" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Infer that model confidence proves the decision is fair.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-08-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-08-e" name="p07-08" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Remove the appeal route to prevent disagreement with the model.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-08-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-09" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">9.</span> A protective action costs 3 and prevents an event loss of 20 completely. There are no other effects. Group A has event probability 0.1 and group B 0.3. Under expected-loss minimization, which policy fits?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-a" name="p07-09" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Randomize equally because neither probability exceeds 0.5.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-b" name="p07-09" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Act for neither group.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-c" name="p07-09" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Act for A only.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-d" name="p07-09" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Act for B only.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-09-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-09-e" name="p07-09" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Act for both groups.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-09-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p07-10" aria-describedby="quiz-p07-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">10.</span> A program has one available place and the same cost for either recipient. Reliable causal estimates say it reduces A&#x27;s event risk from 40% to 35% and B&#x27;s from 25% to 10%. If the sole objective is to maximize expected events prevented, who should receive the place?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-a"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-a" name="p07-10" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Neither, because risk is not reduced to zero.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-b"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-b" name="p07-10" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> B, because the expected reduction is 15 percentage points.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-c"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-c" name="p07-10" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A, because treated risk remains 35%.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-d"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-d" name="p07-10" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> A, because baseline risk is 40%.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p07-10-e"><input type="radio" id="p07-10-e" name="p07-10" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Either, because the program costs the same.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p07-10-result" hidden></p></fieldset>

<details class="practice-key" id="answers-p07"><summary>Answers and explanations</summary><ol class="practice-answer-list">
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p07-01"><h3>Question 1: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Send more reminders about why the service matters. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Memory and motivation are already present.</dd>
<dt>B. Assume abandonment reveals lack of interest. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The stem states interest and identifies another cause.</dd>
<dt>C. Provide a workable identity-check route on the devices people use. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The bottleneck is practical ability at a specific step.</dd>
<dt>D. Hide the identity requirement until the final step. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Concealment does not make the requirement feasible.</dd>
<dt>E. Increase the number of motivational slogans. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Slogans do not fix the technical barrier.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a>. <a href="#p07-01">Back to question 1</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p07-02"><h3>Question 2: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Decision costs should be removed from the analysis. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Those costs are essential to the choice.</dd>
<dt>B. Forecast accuracy determines a unique policy for every person. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Different consequences can justify different actions.</dd>
<dt>C. A shared prediction can support different decisions when consequences differ. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Action thresholds depend on costs and benefits as well as probabilities.</dd>
<dt>D. One forecast must be numerically incorrect. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The forecast is shared; valuations differ.</dd>
<dt>E. The teams must disagree about the definition of rain. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>No such disagreement is specified.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.html">Chapter 41</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-02">Back to question 2</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p07-03"><h3>Question 3: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Both are informational defaults. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Neither necessarily preselects a menu option.</dd>
<dt>B. Both establish that a habit has already formed. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>An intervention is not evidence of learned automaticity.</dd>
<dt>C. The first removes choice; the second only changes wording. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reverses their practical effects.</dd>
<dt>D. The first is a mandate; the second is merely a prediction. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The reminder does not mandate, and the restriction changes choices.</dd>
<dt>E. The first prompts action; the second is a commitment device. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A reminder supplies a cue, while a restriction changes later feasible behavior.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a>. <a href="#p07-03">Back to question 3</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p07-04"><h3>Question 4: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Accept whichever estimate is stated with more confidence. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Confidence can be miscalibrated.</dd>
<dt>B. Average the estimates automatically without inspecting shared errors. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Averaging need not resolve a systematic or input error.</dd>
<dt>C. Choose the AI because computational complexity establishes validity. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Complexity is not a performance test.</dd>
<dt>D. Replace the recorded human estimates with their post-AI revisions. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This erases the independent starting point needed for the audit.</dd>
<dt>E. Check inputs and assumptions, then compare both methods on relevant cases. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Independence makes the disagreement informative; comparative evidence can guide resolution.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.html">Chapter 41</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-04">Back to question 4</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p07-05"><h3>Question 5: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Evaluate only whether the button was clicked faster. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Click speed is still further from the intended benefit.</dd>
<dt>B. Assume higher activity guarantees higher welfare. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Activity and welfare are distinct targets.</dd>
<dt>C. Track submissions, eligibility, actual service delivery, delays, and user costs. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>A proximal action metric can improve while downstream outcomes deteriorate.</dd>
<dt>D. Use submission counts as the sole success measure. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This ignores the newly identified consequences.</dd>
<dt>E. Drop ineligible applications from every report without recording them. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Their processing burden remains relevant.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-05">Back to question 5</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p07-06"><h3>Question 6: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Keep only examples where the aid and manager agreed. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Agreement-based selection excludes important failures.</dd>
<dt>B. Compare easy cases using the aid with hard cases under the old process. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Case difficulty is confounded with the aid.</dd>
<dt>C. Replace the original records with the aid&#x27;s rewritten summaries. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>That obscures the evidence needed to reconstruct performance.</dd>
<dt>D. Choose the success metric after seeing which result looks best. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Post hoc selection can exaggerate improvement.</dd>
<dt>E. Predefine outcomes and randomly assign comparable cases to the two workflows. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Predefined criteria and randomized allocation support a causal comparison of the workflows.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.html">Chapter 41</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-06">Back to question 6</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p07-07"><h3>Question 7: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Require a forfeitable deposit for missing a scheduled session. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This conflicts with the preference against financial penalties and fixed timing.</dd>
<dt>B. Repeat instruction on an exercise she already performs correctly. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Additional skill training does not target the specified boredom.</dd>
<dt>C. Publish a league table of other people&#x27;s attendance. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Social comparison does not directly supply the desired immediate enjoyment.</dd>
<dt>D. Add an extra reminder at a fixed time every day. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The stated barrier is enjoyment, not forgetting.</dd>
<dt>E. Pair exercise with a favorite audiobook reserved for those sessions. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Temptation bundling adds immediate enjoyment without fixed timing or a financial penalty.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/39-behavior-design.html">Chapter 39</a> · <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a>. <a href="#p07-07">Back to question 7</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p07-08"><h3>Question 8: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Treat past labels as correct because they are numerous. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Sample size does not establish label validity.</dd>
<dt>B. Audit labels and criteria; assign an accountable owner and review route. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Predictions can reproduce historical judgments; authorization and correction remain human responsibilities.</dd>
<dt>C. Use a more fluent explanation instead of checking the label process. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Presentation cannot repair a flawed target.</dd>
<dt>D. Infer that model confidence proves the decision is fair. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Confidence does not validate the target or fairness standard.</dd>
<dt>E. Remove the appeal route to prevent disagreement with the model. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This blocks correction of consequential mistakes.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.html">Chapter 41</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-08">Back to question 8</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p07-09"><h3>Question 9: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Randomize equally because neither probability exceeds 0.5. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The threshold is 3/20 = 0.15, not one half.</dd>
<dt>B. Act for neither group. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>For B the expected benefit exceeds the cost.</dd>
<dt>C. Act for A only. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reverses the comparison of avoided loss with cost.</dd>
<dt>D. Act for B only. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Expected avoided losses are 2 for A and 6 for B; only B exceeds the cost 3.</dd>
<dt>E. Act for both groups. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>For A the certain cost exceeds the expected avoided loss.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-09">Back to question 9</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p07-10"><h3>Question 10: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Neither, because risk is not reduced to zero. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Partial risk reduction still serves the stated objective.</dd>
<dt>B. B, because the expected reduction is 15 percentage points. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>B&#x27;s estimated benefit exceeds A&#x27;s five-point reduction.</dd>
<dt>C. A, because treated risk remains 35%. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Remaining risk does not measure the benefit of treatment.</dd>
<dt>D. A, because baseline risk is 40%. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Highest baseline risk is not the same as greatest preventable risk.</dd>
<dt>E. Either, because the program costs the same. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Equal cost does not erase the unequal benefits.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/40-choice-architecture.html">Chapter 40</a> · <a href="../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.html">Chapter 42</a>. <a href="#p07-10">Back to question 10</a></p></li>
</ol></details></form>

::: {.content-visible when-format="epub"}
Choose one answer (A–E) for each of the 10 questions. Record all your choices before following the link to the answer key. Each question is worth one point.

::: {#p07-01 .practice-question}
**Question 1.** People remember to apply for a service and want it, but cannot complete a required identity check on their phones. Which change best matches the observed barrier?

A) Send more reminders about why the service matters.
B) Assume abandonment reveals lack of interest.
C) Provide a workable identity-check route on the devices people use.
D) Hide the identity requirement until the final step.
E) Increase the number of motivational slogans.

:::

::: {#p07-02 .practice-question}
**Question 2.** Two teams share the same rain forecast but choose different umbrella policies because carrying an umbrella has different costs for them. What does this illustrate?

A) Decision costs should be removed from the analysis.
B) Forecast accuracy determines a unique policy for every person.
C) A shared prediction can support different decisions when consequences differ.
D) One forecast must be numerically incorrect.
E) The teams must disagree about the definition of rain.

:::

::: {#p07-03 .practice-question}
**Question 3.** One intervention sends a reminder at the intended action time. Another is a voluntarily chosen restriction preventing access to a competing activity. Which distinction is correct?

A) Both are informational defaults.
B) Both establish that a habit has already formed.
C) The first removes choice; the second only changes wording.
D) The first is a mandate; the second is merely a prediction.
E) The first prompts action; the second is a commitment device.

:::

::: {#p07-04 .practice-question}
**Question 4.** A panel records human estimates before seeing an AI forecast. They disagree strongly. Which next step best uses this disagreement?

A) Accept whichever estimate is stated with more confidence.
B) Average the estimates automatically without inspecting shared errors.
C) Choose the AI because computational complexity establishes validity.
D) Replace the recorded human estimates with their post-AI revisions.
E) Check inputs and assumptions, then compare both methods on relevant cases.

:::

::: {#p07-05 .practice-question}
**Question 5.** A redesigned application page increases submissions but also increases ineligible applications and processing delays. Which evaluation best assesses the full decision path?

A) Evaluate only whether the button was clicked faster.
B) Assume higher activity guarantees higher welfare.
C) Track submissions, eligibility, actual service delivery, delays, and user costs.
D) Use submission counts as the sole success measure.
E) Drop ineligible applications from every report without recording them.

:::

::: {#p07-06 .practice-question}
**Question 6.** A team wants to test a new decision aid. Which plan best supports learning whether it improves the current process?

A) Keep only examples where the aid and manager agreed.
B) Compare easy cases using the aid with hard cases under the old process.
C) Replace the original records with the aid's rewritten summaries.
D) Choose the success metric after seeing which result looks best.
E) Predefine outcomes and randomly assign comparable cases to the two workflows.

:::

::: {#p07-07 .practice-question}
**Question 7.** A reader can exercise safely and remembers the plan, but finds sessions dull. She wants to keep flexible timing and avoid financial penalties. Which design best matches these preferences?

A) Require a forfeitable deposit for missing a scheduled session.
B) Repeat instruction on an exercise she already performs correctly.
C) Publish a league table of other people's attendance.
D) Add an extra reminder at a fixed time every day.
E) Pair exercise with a favorite audiobook reserved for those sessions.

:::

::: {#p07-08 .practice-question}
**Question 8.** A model recommends denying a request, but its training labels reflect past administrative decisions that may contain errors. What is the most important governance step?

A) Treat past labels as correct because they are numerous.
B) Audit labels and criteria; assign an accountable owner and review route.
C) Use a more fluent explanation instead of checking the label process.
D) Infer that model confidence proves the decision is fair.
E) Remove the appeal route to prevent disagreement with the model.

:::

::: {#p07-09 .practice-question}
**Question 9.** A protective action costs 3 and prevents an event loss of 20 completely. There are no other effects. Group A has event probability 0.1 and group B 0.3. Under expected-loss minimization, which policy fits?

A) Randomize equally because neither probability exceeds 0.5.
B) Act for neither group.
C) Act for A only.
D) Act for B only.
E) Act for both groups.

:::

::: {#p07-10 .practice-question}
**Question 10.** A program has one available place and the same cost for either recipient. Reliable causal estimates say it reduces A's event risk from 40% to 35% and B's from 25% to 10%. If the sole objective is to maximize expected events prevented, who should receive the place?

A) Neither, because risk is not reduced to zero.
B) B, because the expected reduction is 15 percentage points.
C) A, because treated risk remains 35%.
D) A, because baseline risk is 40%.
E) Either, because the program costs the same.

:::

[Finished the set? Check the answers and explanations.](#answers-p07)

::: {#answers-p07 .practice-answer-key}
**Answers and explanations**

Count one point for each correct answer, then review the explanations for any alternatives you considered.

**Question 1: C.**

- **A. Send more reminders about why the service matters. (Incorrect)** Memory and motivation are already present.
- **B. Assume abandonment reveals lack of interest. (Incorrect)** The stem states interest and identifies another cause.
- **C. Provide a workable identity-check route on the devices people use. (Correct)** The bottleneck is practical ability at a specific step.
- **D. Hide the identity requirement until the final step. (Incorrect)** Concealment does not make the requirement feasible.
- **E. Increase the number of motivational slogans. (Incorrect)** Slogans do not fix the technical barrier.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd). [Back to question 1](#p07-01).

**Question 2: C.**

- **A. Decision costs should be removed from the analysis. (Incorrect)** Those costs are essential to the choice.
- **B. Forecast accuracy determines a unique policy for every person. (Incorrect)** Different consequences can justify different actions.
- **C. A shared prediction can support different decisions when consequences differ. (Correct)** Action thresholds depend on costs and benefits as well as probabilities.
- **D. One forecast must be numerically incorrect. (Incorrect)** The forecast is shared; valuations differ.
- **E. The teams must disagree about the definition of rain. (Incorrect)** No such disagreement is specified.

Review: [Chapter 41](../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 2](#p07-02).

**Question 3: E.**

- **A. Both are informational defaults. (Incorrect)** Neither necessarily preselects a menu option.
- **B. Both establish that a habit has already formed. (Incorrect)** An intervention is not evidence of learned automaticity.
- **C. The first removes choice; the second only changes wording. (Incorrect)** This reverses their practical effects.
- **D. The first is a mandate; the second is merely a prediction. (Incorrect)** The reminder does not mandate, and the restriction changes choices.
- **E. The first prompts action; the second is a commitment device. (Correct)** A reminder supplies a cue, while a restriction changes later feasible behavior.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd). [Back to question 3](#p07-03).

**Question 4: E.**

- **A. Accept whichever estimate is stated with more confidence. (Incorrect)** Confidence can be miscalibrated.
- **B. Average the estimates automatically without inspecting shared errors. (Incorrect)** Averaging need not resolve a systematic or input error.
- **C. Choose the AI because computational complexity establishes validity. (Incorrect)** Complexity is not a performance test.
- **D. Replace the recorded human estimates with their post-AI revisions. (Incorrect)** This erases the independent starting point needed for the audit.
- **E. Check inputs and assumptions, then compare both methods on relevant cases. (Correct)** Independence makes the disagreement informative; comparative evidence can guide resolution.

Review: [Chapter 41](../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 4](#p07-04).

**Question 5: C.**

- **A. Evaluate only whether the button was clicked faster. (Incorrect)** Click speed is still further from the intended benefit.
- **B. Assume higher activity guarantees higher welfare. (Incorrect)** Activity and welfare are distinct targets.
- **C. Track submissions, eligibility, actual service delivery, delays, and user costs. (Correct)** A proximal action metric can improve while downstream outcomes deteriorate.
- **D. Use submission counts as the sole success measure. (Incorrect)** This ignores the newly identified consequences.
- **E. Drop ineligible applications from every report without recording them. (Incorrect)** Their processing burden remains relevant.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 5](#p07-05).

**Question 6: E.**

- **A. Keep only examples where the aid and manager agreed. (Incorrect)** Agreement-based selection excludes important failures.
- **B. Compare easy cases using the aid with hard cases under the old process. (Incorrect)** Case difficulty is confounded with the aid.
- **C. Replace the original records with the aid's rewritten summaries. (Incorrect)** That obscures the evidence needed to reconstruct performance.
- **D. Choose the success metric after seeing which result looks best. (Incorrect)** Post hoc selection can exaggerate improvement.
- **E. Predefine outcomes and randomly assign comparable cases to the two workflows. (Correct)** Predefined criteria and randomized allocation support a causal comparison of the workflows.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 41](../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 6](#p07-06).

**Question 7: E.**

- **A. Require a forfeitable deposit for missing a scheduled session. (Incorrect)** This conflicts with the preference against financial penalties and fixed timing.
- **B. Repeat instruction on an exercise she already performs correctly. (Incorrect)** Additional skill training does not target the specified boredom.
- **C. Publish a league table of other people's attendance. (Incorrect)** Social comparison does not directly supply the desired immediate enjoyment.
- **D. Add an extra reminder at a fixed time every day. (Incorrect)** The stated barrier is enjoyment, not forgetting.
- **E. Pair exercise with a favorite audiobook reserved for those sessions. (Correct)** Temptation bundling adds immediate enjoyment without fixed timing or a financial penalty.

Review: [Chapter 39](../chapters/39-behavior-design.qmd) · [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd). [Back to question 7](#p07-07).

**Question 8: B.**

- **A. Treat past labels as correct because they are numerous. (Incorrect)** Sample size does not establish label validity.
- **B. Audit labels and criteria; assign an accountable owner and review route. (Correct)** Predictions can reproduce historical judgments; authorization and correction remain human responsibilities.
- **C. Use a more fluent explanation instead of checking the label process. (Incorrect)** Presentation cannot repair a flawed target.
- **D. Infer that model confidence proves the decision is fair. (Incorrect)** Confidence does not validate the target or fairness standard.
- **E. Remove the appeal route to prevent disagreement with the model. (Incorrect)** This blocks correction of consequential mistakes.

Review: [Chapter 41](../chapters/41-decision-hygiene.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 8](#p07-08).

**Question 9: D.**

- **A. Randomize equally because neither probability exceeds 0.5. (Incorrect)** The threshold is 3/20 = 0.15, not one half.
- **B. Act for neither group. (Incorrect)** For B the expected benefit exceeds the cost.
- **C. Act for A only. (Incorrect)** This reverses the comparison of avoided loss with cost.
- **D. Act for B only. (Correct)** Expected avoided losses are 2 for A and 6 for B; only B exceeds the cost 3.
- **E. Act for both groups. (Incorrect)** For A the certain cost exceeds the expected avoided loss.

Review: [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 9](#p07-09).

**Question 10: B.**

- **A. Neither, because risk is not reduced to zero. (Incorrect)** Partial risk reduction still serves the stated objective.
- **B. B, because the expected reduction is 15 percentage points. (Correct)** B's estimated benefit exceeds A's five-point reduction.
- **C. A, because treated risk remains 35%. (Incorrect)** Remaining risk does not measure the benefit of treatment.
- **D. A, because baseline risk is 40%. (Incorrect)** Highest baseline risk is not the same as greatest preventable risk.
- **E. Either, because the program costs the same. (Incorrect)** Equal cost does not erase the unequal benefits.

Review: [Chapter 40](../chapters/40-choice-architecture.qmd) · [Chapter 42](../chapters/42-deciding-with-data-and-ai.qmd). [Back to question 10](#p07-10).

:::
